candidate.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — transmission precautions and safe transfer communication
candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — CRE containment
candidate.educational_objective: Apply current CRE infection-control and interfacility communication practices to prevent transmission.

options.A: Maintain Isolation and Contact Precautions and ensure the receiving facility is notified of the client's CRE colonization status
options.B: Discontinue transmission-based precautions because colonized clients cannot transmit CRE
options.C: Use Airborne Precautions because CRE is primarily spread by airborne droplet nuclei
options.D: Withhold the CRE information from the receiving facility unless the client develops a symptomatic infection

candidate.rationale: Current CDC CRE guidance recommends Isolation and Contact Precautions in acute-care settings and emphasizes communication of CRE infection or colonization status during interfacility transfer. Colonized clients can contribute to transmission, and CRE spreads mainly through contact with contaminated hands, wounds, stool, equipment, or the healthcare environment rather than the airborne route.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Acute-care CRE colonization requires targeted contact-based precautions and communication during transfer.
candidate.source_locator: Infection prevention and control — Isolation and Contact Precautions in acute care; Safe patient transfers — notify receiving facility about CRE infection or colonization
candidate.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
candidate.stem: A client in an acute-care hospital is identified as colonized with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and is being transferred to another facility. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
